title: An AI exec is stepping down, citing workload and stress. Here's how 10 business leaders stave off burnout.
excerpt: "I ultimately have to admit that the amount of consistent stress and workload have pushed me beyond what my health can sustain physically," Lilian Weng wrote.
content_html:
Burnout stalks even the most accomplished operators.

On Tuesday, Lilian Weng, a cofounder of Thinking Machines Lab and former OpenAI safety executive, announced her resignation from her role.

In a note to colleagues, later shared on X, she wrote that seven months of recurring illness, made worse by the relentless pace of startup life, had left her unable to give the job the full effort she felt it demanded.

"After thinking about it for several months, I ultimately have to admit that the amount of consistent stress and workload have pushed me beyond what my health can sustain physically," Weng wrote. She said she hopes to return in a more scoped role at a calmer workplace.

Here's how 10 other business leaders have said they keep burnout at bay.

Evan Spiegel, Michael Dell, and Jamie Siminoff: build guardrails into the grind

Some leaders keep grinding but fence off pieces of their lives.

Snap CEO Evan Spiegel, who calls his seven-day-a-week schedule "completely insane," says Sundays are non-negotiable: church, brunch, and an afternoon with his four kids.

Michael Dell's guardrail is levity. The Dell Technologies founder has said there's a diminishing return on hours worked in a day, and anyone in it for the long haul needs a mix of working, playing, and relaxing.

Ring founder Jamie Siminoff opts for what he calls "work-life fusion," folding family into the job, for example, by bringing them along on business trips.

Arianna Huffington and Jeff Bezos: Treat rest as an asset

Others treat rest itself as the strategy.

Two years after founding The Huffington Post, Arianna Huffington collapsed from exhaustion at her desk, breaking her cheekbone. She said in a LinkedIn post in 2014 that the fall convinced her that equating success with burnout is a "collective delusion." She later set up a company, Thrive Global, focused on well-being.

Jeff Bezos frames rest as a fiduciary duty. "Eight hours of sleep makes a big difference for me," the Amazon founder told Huffington's Thrive Global, arguing that an executive is paid to make a few high-quality decisions, and shortchanging sleep just yields more tired, lower-quality ones.

Indra Nooyi and Sheryl Sandberg: accept the trade-offs

Some leaders sidestep burnout by abandoning an impossible standard.

"I don't think women can have it all. We pretend we can have it all," Indra Nooyi, then the CEO of PepsiCo, said in 2014. Her answer was to stop pretending: to treat each day as a series of explicit trade-offs among CEO, wife, and mother, and to co-opt family and colleagues to fill the gaps.

Former Meta COO Sheryl Sandberg made a similar case in "Lean In," calling "having it all" perhaps the greatest trap ever set for women. She has also defended leaving the office at 5:30 p.m. for family dinner.

Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, and Lloyd Blankfein: life's too short

A few notable business leaders have said they refuse to let work swallow everything else.

At Berkshire Hathaway's 2023 annual meeting, Warren Buffett and his late partner, Charlie Munger, contrasted themselves with Elon Musk, whom Munger said succeeds by insisting on unreasonably extreme goals. "Warren and I are looking for the easy job," Munger said. "We don't want that much failure."

Munger warned graduates away from grinding careers, too, saying that winning a pie-eating contest just means eating more pie, and "life is too short to just do nothing but eat pie."

Buffett's advice was to work backward from the end: "write your obituary and try and figure out how to live up to it." He kept the job he loved until handing Berkshire's reins to Greg Abel this past January, at age 95.

Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein got similar advice decades ago: In his memoir "Streetwise," he recalled that when he made partner, he was told that if his obituary ran nine paragraphs, no more than three should be about Goldman. He retired in 2018 and has leaned into the other six: philanthropy, family, and, by his own account, thoroughly enjoying not having to travel for work.

content_html_zh:
即使是最有成就的操作员也会感到倦怠。

周二，Thinking Machines Lab 联合创始人、前 OpenAI 安全主管 Lilian Weng 宣布辞去职务。

在后来在 X 上分享的给同事的一封信中，她写道，七个月的病情反复发作，再加上创业生活的无情节奏，让她无法为这份工作付出她认为需要的全部努力。

翁写道：“经过几个月的思考，我最终不得不承认，持续的压力和工作量已经超出了我的健康所能承受的范围。” 她说，她希望回到一个更加平静的工作场所，担任更广泛的角色。

埃文·斯皮格尔、迈克尔·戴尔和杰米·西米诺夫：在磨难中建造护栏

有些领导者一直在苦苦挣扎，但却把自己的生活中的一些事情隔离开来。

Snap 首席执行官埃文·斯皮格尔 (Evan Spiegel) 称自己每周 7 天的日程安排“完全疯狂”，他表示周日是没有商量余地的：去教堂、吃早午餐，以及与四个孩子共度一个下午。

迈克尔·戴尔的护栏是轻浮的。 这位戴尔科技公司创始人表示，一天工作时间的回报正在递减，任何人长期工作都需要工作、娱乐和放松的结合。

Ring 创始人杰米·西米诺夫 (Jamie Siminoff) 选择了他所谓的“工作与生活融合”，将家庭融入到工作中，例如，带家人一起出差。

阿里安娜·赫芬顿和杰夫·贝佐斯：将休息视为资产

其他人则将休息本身视为策略。

创办《赫芬顿邮报》两年后，阿里安娜·赫芬顿因精疲力尽而倒在办公桌前，导致颧骨骨折。 她在 2014 年的 LinkedIn 帖子中表示，这次摔倒让她相信，将成功等同于倦怠是一种“集体错觉”。 后来她成立了一家名为 Thrive Global 的公司，专注于福祉。

杰夫·贝索斯将休息视为一项信托义务。 这位亚马逊创始人告诉赫芬顿的《Thrive Global》，“八小时的睡眠对我来说意义重大。”他认为，高管的报酬是为了做出一些高质量的决定，而缩短睡眠时间只会导致更疲劳、质量更低的决策。

英德拉·努伊和谢丽尔·桑德伯格：接受权衡

一些领导者通过放弃不可能的标准来避免倦怠。

“我不认为女性可以拥有这一切。 我们假装我们可以拥有一切，”时任百事公司首席执行官的英德拉·努伊 (Indra Nooyi) 在 2014 年说道。 她的答案是停止假装：将每一天视为首席执行官、妻子和母亲之间一系列明确的权衡，并选择家人和同事来填补空白。

Meta 前首席运营官谢丽尔·桑德伯格 (Sheryl Sandberg) 在《向前一步》(Lean In) 中提出了类似的案例，称“拥有一切”可能是有史以来为女性设置的最大陷阱。 她还为下午 5:30 离开办公室辩护。 家庭晚餐。

沃伦·巴菲特、查理·芒格和劳埃德·布兰克费恩：生命太短暂

一些著名的商界领袖表示，他们拒绝让工作吞噬其他一切。

在伯克希尔·哈撒韦公司 2023 年年会上，沃伦·巴菲特和他已故的合伙人查理·芒格将自己与埃隆·马斯克进行了对比，芒格表示，埃隆·马斯克之所以成功是因为坚持不合理的极端目标。 “沃伦和我正在寻找一份轻松的工作，”芒格说。 “我们不希望有那么多失败。”

芒格也警告毕业生不要从事艰苦的职业，他说赢得吃馅饼比赛就意味着吃更多的馅饼，而“生命太短，除了吃馅饼什么都不做”。

巴菲特的建议是从最后开始倒推：“写下你的讣告，并尝试找出如何实现它。” 他一直保留着自己热爱的工作，直到今年 1 月将伯克希尔的管理权交给了 95 岁的格雷格·阿贝尔 (Greg Abel)。

高盛前首席执行官劳埃德·布兰克费恩（Lloyd Blankfein）几十年前就得到了类似的建议：在他的回忆录《Streetwise》中，他回忆道，当他成为合伙人时，他被告知，如果他的讣告有九段，关于高盛的内容不应超过三段。 他于 2018 年退休，并专注于其他六件事：慈善事业、家庭，而且据他自己说，他非常享受不用出差工作的感觉。
